    13	/** Injectable session factory — the seam a route test scripts instead of opening a real socket.
    14	 *  Same seam `mcp-federation/bootstrap.ts`'s own `connect` parameter provides, for the identical reason:
    15	 *  the protocol code under test should be the real thing, not a second hand-rolled fake of it. */
    16	export type ExternalMcpProbeSessionFactory = (
    17	  required: { spec: McpHttpLaunchSpec; requestTimeoutMs: number },
    18	  optional?: Record<string, never>,
    19	) => Promise<McpSessionPort>;
    20	
    21	export type ExternalMcpProbeServiceDeps = Pick<ExternalMcpToolDeps, "workspaceId" | "clock" | "externalMcpServerRepo" | "siteAssistantSecretSealer"> & {
    22	  /**
    23	   * Optional: only consulted for a connection whose `authMode` is `"oauth"`.
    24	   * `readEnabledExternalMcpConfigs`'s own `oauth` parameter is equally optional, for the same
    25	   * reason — a deployment that has never wired an OAuth service can still probe a `none`/
    26	   * `static_env` connection, so this route must not demand the service just to run at all.
    27	   */
    28	  readonly externalMcpOAuth?: ExternalMcpOAuthService;
    29	  /** Defaults to the real hosted MCP client. See {@link ExternalMcpProbeSessionFactory}. */
    30	  readonly connect?: ExternalMcpProbeSessionFactory;
    31	};
    32	
    33	/** The real session factory: one handshake against the resolved hosted endpoint, bounded by the
    34	 *  connection's own `connectTimeoutMs`. Deliberately NOT the same bound `bootstrap.ts`'s
    35	 *  `defaultConnect` uses for the identical transport: that session is long-lived and its bound
    36	 *  governs every later `tools/call` too, so it uses `callTimeoutMs`. This one issues an `initialize`
    37	 *  handshake via {@link connectMcpHttpSession} followed by this route's own single `listTools`
    38	 *  call, then is closed immediately after — for THIS session, `connectTimeoutMs` bounds the
    39	 *  handshake and is the correct bound rather than a reused wrong one.
    40	 *  @complexity O(1) beyond the remote's round-trip. */
    41	async function defaultProbeConnect({ spec, requestTimeoutMs }: { spec: McpHttpLaunchSpec; requestTimeoutMs: number }, _optional = {}): Promise<McpSessionPort> {
    42	  return connectMcpHttpSession({ exchange: createFetchMcpHttpExchange({ fetch }), spec, requestTimeoutMs });
    43	}
    44	
    45	/** One resolved, probeable target: the trust-tier config `describeRemoteToolSurface` needs, and the
    46	 *  hosted launch spec to connect with. */
    47	interface ProbeTarget {
    48	  readonly federationConfig: FederatedMcpConnectionConfig;
    49	  readonly launch: McpHttpLaunchSpec;
    50	}
    51	
    52	/** One outcome of {@link resolveProbeTarget}: either a usable target, or a response this route
    53	 *  should send verbatim without ever attempting a connection. Modelled as a union rather than
    54	 *  throwing, because every branch here is an ordinary, expected outcome (unknown id, wrong
    55	 *  transport, disabled row, stale authorization) — none of them is exceptional. */
    56	type ProbeTargetResolution = { readonly ok: true; readonly target: ProbeTarget } | { readonly ok: false; readonly status: number; readonly body: Record<string, unknown> };
    57	
    58	/** Refuses a `stdio` row (D-7), a disabled row, and the common `needs_reauth` case, all from the
    59	 *  record alone — before any credential is ever resolved. Split out of {@link resolveProbeTarget}
    60	 *  purely to keep that function's complexity under the shop ceiling.
    61	 *  @returns The response to send, or `null` to continue resolving.
    62	 *  @complexity O(1). */
    63	function refuseBeforeResolving({ record, serverId }: { record: ExternalMcpServerRecord; serverId: string }, _optional = {}): Extract<ProbeTargetResolution, { ok: false }> | null {
    64	  if (record.transport === "stdio") {
    65	    return {
    66	      ok: false,
    67	      status: 400,
    68	      body: {
    69	        error: "probe is not available for local-command servers yet — type tool names directly instead",
    70	        code: "PROBE_UNSUPPORTED_TRANSPORT",
    71	        details: { field: "transport" },
    72	      },
    73	    };
    74	  }
    75	  if (!record.enabled) {
    76	    return {
    77	      ok: false,
    78	      status: 400,
    79	      body: { error: "this server is disabled — enable it before probing", code: "MCP_SERVER_DISABLED", details: { field: "enabled" } },
    80	    };
    81	  }
    82	  if (resolveExternalMcpAuthMode(record) === "oauth" && resolveExternalMcpOAuthStatus(record) === "needs_reauth") {
    83	    const error = new ExternalMcpReauthRequiredError({ serverId, label: record.label });
    84	    return { ok: false, status: 409, body: { error: error.message, code: error.code, details: { retryable: false, settingsLink: error.settingsLink } } };
    85	  }
    86	  return null;
    87	}
    88	
    89	/** Turns one `readEnabledExternalMcpConfigs` MISS (the server resolved to neither a usable config
    90	 *  nor — because it is enabled and past the early checks — anything but a failure entry) into a
    91	 *  response. Split out of {@link resolveProbeTarget} purely to keep that function's complexity under
    92	 *  the shop ceiling.
    93	 *  @complexity O(1) given the caller already located `failure`. */
    94	function respondToResolutionFailure({ serverId, reason }: { serverId: string; reason: string }, _optional = {}): Extract<ProbeTargetResolution, { ok: false }> {
    95	  /** `true` only for the fixed prose {@link resolveProbeTarget}'s failure branch and
    96	   *  `external-mcp-oauth.ts`'s `ExternalMcpReauthRequiredError` share today — see this file's header
    97	   *  on the residual race this covers: a row whose STORED status is `"connected"` but whose live token
    98	   *  refresh fails with an invalid grant during this exact probe call. The common case (a row already
    99	   *  parked `needs_reauth`) never reaches this function — {@link refuseBeforeResolving} catches the
   100	   *  stored status directly, before `readEnabledExternalMcpConfigs` is ever called. A future wording
   101	   *  change in either source string would silently widen this to the generic 502 branch instead of
   102	   *  409, never the other direction — the safer failure mode for a coupling this loose. */
   103	  if (reason.includes("authorization expired or was revoked")) {
   104	    return {
   105	      ok: false,
   106	      status: 409,
   107	      body: { error: reason, code: "EXTERNAL_MCP_REAUTH_REQUIRED", details: { retryable: false, settingsLink: externalMcpSettingsDeepLink({ serverId }) } },
   108	    };
   109	  }
   110	  return { ok: false, status: 502, body: { error: reason, code: "MCP_SERVER_UNREACHABLE" } };
   111	}
   112	
   113	/** Resolves one `serverId` into a probeable target, or the exact response to send instead. Never
   114	 *  spawns a child process — see this file's D-7 header. Built on `readEnabledExternalMcpConfigs`/
   115	 *  `toResolvedFederatedConnections`, the same pair the daemon's own boot path resolves credentials
   116	 *  through, so a probe's target is derived exactly the way a real connect would be, rather than by a
   117	 *  second, parallel reading of the row.
   118	 *  @complexity O(n) in the workspace's configured server count — bounded by the store's own
   119	 *  per-workspace server cap. */
   120	async function resolveProbeTarget({ deps, serverId }: { deps: ExternalMcpProbeServiceDeps; serverId: string }, _optional = {}): Promise<ProbeTargetResolution> {
   121	  const record = await deps.externalMcpServerRepo.findByServerId({ workspaceId: deps.workspaceId, serverId });
   122	  if (!record) {
   123	    return { ok: false, status: 400, body: { error: `no external MCP server is configured as '${serverId}'`, code: "INVALID_MCP_SERVER", details: { field: "id" } } };
   124	  }
   125	
   126	  const earlyRefusal = refuseBeforeResolving({ record, serverId });
   127	  if (earlyRefusal) return earlyRefusal;
   128	
   129	  const { configs, failures } = await readEnabledExternalMcpConfigs(
   130	    { repo: deps.externalMcpServerRepo, sealer: deps.siteAssistantSecretSealer, oauth: deps.externalMcpOAuth?.tokenResolver },
   131	    deps.workspaceId,
   132	  );
   133	
   134	  const config = configs.find((candidate) => candidate.serverId === serverId);
   135	  if (!config) {
   136	    const failure = failures.find((candidate) => candidate.serverId === serverId);
   137	    return respondToResolutionFailure({ serverId, reason: failure?.reason ?? "this server's connection could not be resolved" });
   138	  }
   139	
   140	  const [resolved] = toResolvedFederatedConnections([config]);
   141	  // Defensive, not reachable given the transport check above (`config.transport` mirrors
   142	  // `record.transport` — both come from the same row): the whole point of D-7 is that this route
   143	  // must never launch a child process, and a launch-spec SHAPE check right before connecting is the
   144	  // cheapest possible second guarantee of that, independent of whatever produced `resolved`.
   145	  if (!resolved || !("url" in resolved.launch)) {
   146	    return { ok: false, status: 400, body: { error: "probe is not available for local-command servers yet", code: "PROBE_UNSUPPORTED_TRANSPORT" } };
   147	  }
   148	
   149	  return { ok: true, target: { federationConfig: resolved.config, launch: resolved.launch } };
   150	}
   151	
   152	/** Recognizes the probe's supported opaque HTTP and typed MCP authentication failures. */
   153	function isProbeAuthFailure({ error }: { error: unknown }, _options = {}): boolean {
   154	  const status = error && typeof error === 'object' ? (error as { status?: unknown; statusCode?: unknown }).status ?? (error as { statusCode?: unknown }).statusCode : undefined;
   155	  if (status === 401 || status === 403 || error instanceof McpAuthFailedError) return true;
   156	  return error instanceof McpProtocolError && /with HTTP (401|403)$/.test(error.message);
   157	}
   158	
   159	/** Only real Error instances and recognized protocol messages count as timeouts. */
   160	function isProbeTimeoutFailure({ error }: { error: unknown }, _options = {}): boolean {
   161	  if (!(error instanceof Error)) return false;
   162	  if (error.name === 'AbortError' || error.name === 'TimeoutError') return true;
   163	  return error instanceof McpProtocolError && /request (?:timed out|was aborted)/.test(error.message);
   164	}
   165	
   166	/** Connects once, lists, describes, and closes — the `finally` is the whole safety story for the
   167	 *  outbound session, matching W-002's own framing in the implementation outline. Split out of the
   168	 *  route handler purely to keep it under the shop ceiling.
   169	 *  @complexity O(t) in the remote's advertised tool count, plus one round trip. */
   170	async function runProbe(connect: ExternalMcpProbeSessionFactory, target: ProbeTarget): Promise<{ ok: true; tools: ReturnType<typeof describeRemoteToolSurface> } | { ok: false; kind: "auth" | "timeout" | "unreachable" }> {
   171	  let session: McpSessionPort | undefined;
   172	  try {
   173	    session = await connect({ spec: target.launch, requestTimeoutMs: target.federationConfig.connectTimeoutMs });
   174	    const tools = await session.listTools();
   175	    return { ok: true, tools: describeRemoteToolSurface({ tools, config: target.federationConfig }) };
   176	  } catch (err) {
   177	    // Report the failed connection without logging upstream errors that may contain credentials.
   178	    // Upstream bodies/errors may contain credentials; only the closed category crosses this boundary.
   179	    const auth = isProbeAuthFailure({ error: err });
   180	    const timeout = isProbeTimeoutFailure({ error: err });
   181	    const fallbackKind = timeout ? 'timeout' : 'unreachable';
   182	    return { ok: false, kind: auth ? 'auth' : fallbackKind };
   183	  } finally {
   184	    // The probe result is already decided; closing its optional session is best effort.
   185	    await session?.close({}).catch(() => undefined);
   186	  }
   187	}
   188	
   189	/** Resolves credentials, probes once, then closes. Expected refusals retain the admin response contract.
   190	 * OAuth resolution can refresh and persist a grant, so this operation is not declared read-only.
   191	 * @complexity O(n + t) time and O(n + t) space for saved servers and advertised tools, plus bounded I/O.
   192	 */
   193	export async function probeExternalMcpServer({ deps, serverId }: { deps: ExternalMcpProbeServiceDeps; serverId: string }, _optional = {}) {
   194	  const resolution = await resolveProbeTarget({ deps, serverId });
   195	  if (!resolution.ok) return resolution;
   196	  const outcome = await runProbe(deps.connect ?? defaultProbeConnect, resolution.target);
   197	  if (!outcome.ok) {
   198	    const failure = { auth: { status: 401, code: 'MCP_AUTH_REJECTED' }, timeout: { status: 504, code: 'MCP_TIMEOUT' }, unreachable: { status: 502, code: 'MCP_SERVER_UNREACHABLE' } }[outcome.kind];
   199	    return { ok: false as const, status: failure.status, body: { error: credentialText({ id: outcome.kind }), code: failure.code } };
   200	  }
   201	  return { ok: true as const, body: { tools: outcome.tools, probedAt: new Date(deps.clock.nowMs()).toISOString() } };
   202	}

1	/**
     2	 * @file Event, outbox and transaction-boundary port contracts.
     3	 *
     4	 * Purpose:
     5	 * Defines the stable interfaces that domain/application code depends on to publish events and deliver them reliably.
     6	 *
     7	 * Architectural role:
     8	 * This file is the dependency inversion seam. Hosts provide in-memory or durable implementations and compose them in
     9	 * their composition root. Concrete infrastructure can change without changing feature logic as long as implementations
    10	 * satisfy these types.
    11	 *
    12	 * Design goal:
    13	 * Core/domain code depends on interfaces from this file only, never on concrete infrastructure SDKs or
    14	 * framework-specific implementations.
    15	 */
    16	import type { UUID, ISODateTime } from "../../primitives/index.js";
    17	
    18	/**
    19	 * Immutable domain event emitted by synchronous command handlers and delivered
    20	 * asynchronously via the outbox pipeline.
    21	 */
    22	export interface DomainEvent<TPayload = Record<string, unknown>> {
    23	  /** Unique identifier for the event record. */
    24	  id: UUID;
    25	  /** Stable event name, e.g. `workspace.created`. */
    26	  name: string;
    27	  /** ISO timestamp describing when the event was produced. */
    28	  occurredAt: ISODateTime;
    29	  /** Optional aggregate root identifier related to this event. */
    30	  aggregateId?: UUID;
    31	  /**
    32	   * Tenant/workspace boundary. Required: every domain event belongs to a
    33	   * workspace. Platform-level events must be a deliberate future
    34	   * decision, not an omission.
    35	   */
    36	  workspaceId: UUID;
    37	  /**
    38	   * Principal (user or AI agent) that caused this event. Reserved change-set
    39	   * vocabulary; optional until the identity library lands.
    40	   */
    41	  actorId?: UUID;
    42	  /**
    43	   * Change set this event belongs to, enabling propose/preview/apply/revert
    44	   * grouping. Reserved change-set vocabulary.
    45	   */
    46	  changeSetId?: UUID;
    47	  /** Event-specific payload. */
    48	  payload: TPayload;
    49	  /** Free-form metadata (trace IDs, source, etc.). */
    50	  metadata?: Record<string, unknown>;
    51	}
    52	
    53	/**
    54	 * Event bus abstraction used by the application layer.
    55	 *
    56	 * This is intentionally generic so implementations can be in-memory, queue-based,
    57	 * broker-based, or provider-managed without changing domain logic.
    58	 */
    59	export interface EventBusPort {
    60	  /** Publish a single event to subscribers. */
    61	  publish<TPayload>(event: DomainEvent<TPayload>): Promise<void>;
    62	  /** Publish multiple events in order. */
    63	  publishBatch<TPayload>(required: { events: Array<DomainEvent<TPayload>> }, optional?: Record<string, never>): Promise<void>;
    64	  /**
    65	   * Subscribe a handler to an event name.
    66	   * Returns an async unsubscriber function.
    67	   */
    68	  subscribe<TPayload>(
    69	    required: { eventName: string; handler: (event: DomainEvent<TPayload>) => Promise<void> },
    70	    optional?: Record<string, never>
    71	  ): Promise<() => Promise<void>>;
    72	  /**
    73	   * Subscribe a handler to every event published on this bus, regardless of name. Additive to
    74	   * `subscribe` — existing per-name callers are unaffected.
    75	   * The Integrations fan-out (`registerWebhookFanout`) is the first real consumer: it narrows
    76	   * by topic itself rather than requiring a fixed list of event names up front.
    77	   */
    78	  subscribeAll(required: { handler: (event: DomainEvent) => Promise<void> }, optional?: Record<string, never>): Promise<() => Promise<void>>;
    79	}
    80	
    81	/**
    82	 * Persisted outbox row used for reliable async event delivery.
    83	 */
    84	export interface OutboxRecord {
    85	  /** Primary key for the outbox row (same as `event.id`). */
    86	  id: UUID;
    87	  /**
    88	   * The full event envelope. The outbox must preserve everything the producer
    89	   * emitted (workspaceId, aggregateId, actorId, occurredAt, metadata) so
    90	   * delivery replays the original event, not a reconstruction.
    91	   */
    92	  event: DomainEvent;
    93	  /** Delivery lifecycle state. */
    94	  status: "pending" | "processing" | "delivered" | "failed";
    95	  /** Number of delivery attempts so far. */
    96	  attempts: number;
    97	  /** Retry eligibility timestamp. */
    98	  nextAttemptAt: ISODateTime;
    99	  /** Most recent delivery failure reason. */
   100	  lastError?: string;
   101	  /** Row creation timestamp. */
   102	  createdAt: ISODateTime;
   103	}
   104	
   105	/**
   106	 * Reliable outbox contract.
   107	 *
   108	 * Command handlers enqueue events here in the same unit of work as the write.
   109	 * A worker later claims and delivers rows to the event bus.
   110	 */
   111	export interface OutboxPort {
   112	  /** Append an event for later delivery. */
   113	  enqueue(event: DomainEvent): Promise<void>;
   114	  /** Claim pending rows for processing. */
   115	  claimPending(required: { batchSize: number; nowIso: ISODateTime }, optional?: Record<string, never>): Promise<OutboxRecord[]>;
   116	  /** Mark a row as delivered. */
   117	  markDelivered(required: { id: UUID }, optional?: Record<string, never>): Promise<void>;
   118	  /**
   119	   * Mark a row as failed and set its next retry time.
   120	   *
   121	   * `nextStatus` is decided by the CALLER (the retry-policy owner, e.g. a worker that tracks an
   122	   * attempt cap) — an implementation must persist exactly what it is told, not re-derive the
   123	   * decision from the row's own stored `attempts` (2026-09-06: this parameter replaced that
   124	   * adapter-side re-derivation, mirroring `WebhookDeliveryRepoPort.markFailed`'s `nextStatus`
   125	   * shape in the host). `"pending"` re-enters the retry queue at `nextAttemptAt`; `"failed"`
   126	   * is terminal — `claimPending` only ever selects `"pending"` rows, so a `"failed"` row is
   127	   * permanently excluded from retry regardless of `nextAttemptAt`.
   128	   */
   129	  markFailed(
   130	    required: {
   131	      id: UUID;
   132	      error: string;
   133	      nextAttemptAt: ISODateTime;
   134	      nextStatus: Extract<OutboxRecord["status"], "pending" | "failed">;
   135	    },
   136	    optional?: Record<string, never>
   137	  ): Promise<void>;
   138	}
   139	
   140	/** Clock and ID generator contracts are owned by the shared kernel primitives. */
   141	
   142	/**
   143	 * Opens/commits/rolls back one transaction around `fn` — the same shape and contract as this
   144	 * codebase's other write chokepoints that need one (`RedirectsWriteDeps.transaction`,
   145	 * `SqliteSettingsRepo.transaction`).
   146	 *
   147	 * `deleteTerm`/`deleteTaxonomy` run their ENTIRE body — every guard read (`findById`,
   148	 * `countChildren`, `countByTerm`) AND every write (`delete`, `revisions.insert`, `outbox.enqueue`)
   149	 * — inside one call to this. Two failure modes this closes that a guard-then-transaction split
   150	 * would not:
   151	 *
   152	 * 1. **TOCTOU on the guard.** A guard read taken BEFORE the transaction opens can go stale the
   153	 *    instant it returns — content can be assigned to the term in the gap between the read and the
   154	 *    delete, and the delete would proceed having checked a now-wrong count. Putting the read
   155	 *    inside the same transaction as the delete is what makes the guard's answer still true at the
   156	 *    moment the delete actually runs.
   157	 * 2. **Partial cascade.** `deleteTaxonomy` deletes N member terms then the taxonomy row itself,
   158	 *    with no FK/CASCADE at the schema level (the host schema — `taxonomies`/`terms`/`entry_terms`/
   159	 *    `taxonomy_revisions` are plain columns, no foreign keys) to undo a mid-cascade failure. A

 * ## What belongs here
 *

 * kit every domain's agent-tool layer builds on. No Express, no `node:*`, no DOM, no concrete

 * ## What belongs in Node-bound domain entries
 *

 * stores, image transformers, and anything importing `node:*` or a native dependency. These
 * adapters depend on core; the reverse is a boundary violation. User-management tool registration
 * composition belongs to its own server entry point.

     4	 * Why this exists: `generate-postgres-schema.ts` proves the two dialects' DDL agree structurally
     5	 * (same tables, same constraints, same indexes). That is necessary but not sufficient — a schema
     6	 * can compile on both dialects and still be wrong in ways structure alone cannot see: an
     7	 * autoincrement column that silently rejects row 2,147,483,648 once real traffic accumulates, a
     8	 * timestamp column that is byte-identical on both sides but ambiguous the moment anyone reads it,
     9	 * an identity sequence left at 1 after a bulk copy that preserved the original row ids, a JSON
    10	 * payload that survives as bytes but not as JSON. Those are semantic facts about specific columns
    11	 * that Drizzle's type system does not encode and the structural generator/parity tests cannot see
    12	 * (see `schema-postgres-parity.test.ts`'s own doc for why "does it look the same" and "does it mean
    13	 * the same thing" are different questions — this file answers the second one).
    14	 *
    15	 * Why "manifest", and why executable rather than a document: per the 2026-08-12 postgres-foundation
    16	 * handoff, this is meant to be the single thing both schema generation and migration verification
    17	 * consume, so the two can never independently drift out of agreement the way two hand-written docs
    18	 * would. A markdown table recording "these columns need bigint" would need someone to remember to
    19	 * update it every time a table is added; this file's structural facts (table/column list, SQLite
    20	 * column kind, primary-key/autoincrement-ness) are instead DERIVED from `schema.sqlite.ts` via the exact
    21	 * same `drizzle-orm/sqlite-core` `getTableConfig()` introspection `generate-postgres-schema.ts`
    22	 * already uses — so those facts cannot drift from the source schema either. Manual review only
    23	 * happens where structure genuinely cannot answer the question (Drizzle has no concept of "this
    24	 * integer column is an unbounded append-only log" — that is a fact about how the product uses the
    25	 * table, not about its declared type), and every such manual judgment lives in one reviewed
    26	 * registry below with its rationale attached, not scattered as tribal knowledge.
    27	 *
    28	 * Scope this round (per the dispatch brief): build the manifest and its migration-verification
    29	 * consumer (`./verify.ts`, deleted 2026-10-03 with no production caller; see development/DELETED-CODE.md),
    30	 * proven against a real local Postgres fixture (`__tests__/migration-manifest-postgres.test.ts`). `classifyPluginColumn` below is a generic
    31	 * convention seam for a *future* Postgres DDL path for plugin-declared tables (`data-module.ts`
    32	 * only targets SQLite today) — it is written and tested now so that path does not have to invent
    33	 * its own semantic conventions later.
    34	 *
    35	 * IMPORTANT — a decision landed underneath this manifest while it was being built, and this doc is
    36	 * being honest about it rather than pretending the two still agree: `REVIEWED_INTEGER_ID_COLUMNS`
    37	 * below was designed as the input `generate-postgres-schema.ts`'s `columnBuilder()` should consume
    38	 * for its `bigint` vs `integer` choice — a narrower allowlist scoped to the handoff's named risk
    39	 * categories (append-only logs + the watermark). Commit `b393752` (concurrent with this task, same
    40	 * session) instead shipped a BROADER, already-merged policy: every one of the schema's 65
    41	 * `SQLiteInteger` columns is `bigint(..., {mode:"number"})` now, not a hand-picked subset — reasoned
    42	 * explicitly against a narrower allowlist like this registry, on two grounds: (1) this generator's
    43	 * own design already commits to kind-based mapping plus exhaustive structural gates specifically so
    44	 * a manually-maintained allowlist can never be the failure mode, and an allowlist is exactly what
    45	 * this registry is; (2) all 11 autoincrement PKs get protected, not only the ones an audit judged
    46	 * "obviously" high-volume — a narrower allowlist would leave e.g. `entry_refs.id`/`entry_terms.id`

    48	 * something the generator still needs to consume; the schema-generation question it was meant to
    49	 * answer is already settled, more conservatively than this registry alone would have required.
    50	 * The registry is kept, with its role changed and its vocabulary corrected to match: it is no longer

    59	 * What this manifest deliberately does NOT do:
    60	 * - It is not a migration completeness signal. See `WATERMARK_IS_NOT_A_MIGRATION_BOUNDARY` below —

    62	 * - It does not change the timestamp representation. Timestamps stay `text` ISO-8601 this round —
    63	 *   see the timestamp representation note for why that is reversible only until a deadline, not indefinitely.
    64	 * - It does not touch FTS5/search. See `DERIVED_OBJECTS` — search is rebuilt, never copied.

    93	/** Every exported Drizzle table in `schema.sqlite.ts`. */

   100	/** Maps each column to its TypeScript property name (`bodyJson`, not `body_json`) by identity, the
   101	 * same recovery technique `generate-postgres-schema.ts`'s `tsPropertyNames` uses — see that file's
   102	 * own doc for why identity lookup rather than a naming-convention guess is required. */
   103	function tsPropertyNames(table: object, columns: readonly SQLiteColumn[]): Map<SQLiteColumn, string> {
   104	  const byColumn = new Map<SQLiteColumn, string>();
   105	  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(table)) {
   106	    const match = columns.find((c) => c === value);
   107	    if (match) byColumn.set(match, key);
   108	  }
   109	  return byColumn;
   110	}

   115	 * file's own bare `SQLiteColumn` import — structurally identical at runtime (the same drizzle-orm
   116	 * class), incompatible only because `Column`'s `config` member is `protected`, which makes

   120	 * here so every call site downstream sees one ordinary `SQLiteColumn[]`, not a repeated cast.

   151	/**
   152	 * The safe-integer ceiling `PgBigInt53` columns are actually subject to, carried as data for the same
   153	 * reason the timestamp representation note below is: a fact someone must not have to remember from a handoff
   154	 * document alone.
   155	 *
   156	 * `bigint(..., { mode: "number" })` (what every `SQLiteInteger` column generates as — see this
   157	 * section's own note above and "GATE A" in migration-manifest.test.ts) routes every value through
   158	 * `Number(value)`. Postgres's `int8` itself can hold up to ~9.2×10^18, but the JS `number` this
   159	 * manifest's own generated schema chose to read it back as cannot represent every int8 value exactly
   160	 * past 2^53 — `9007199254740993` round-trips as `...992`.
   161	 *
   162	 * The fix is NOT `mode: "bigint"`. Two independent auditors flagged that switching modes would make
   163	 * Drizzle return a native JS `BigInt` for these columns instead of `number`, which breaks two things
   164	 * across the API layer, not just here: `JSON.stringify` throws on a `BigInt` with no replacer (every
   165	 * response serializing one of these ids breaks), and JS refuses mixed `Number`/`BigInt` arithmetic
   166	 * (`1n + 1` throws `TypeError`) — every existing call site doing arithmetic on one of these ids would
   167	 * need an audited rewrite. Not attempted this round; `mode: "number"` stays.
   168	 *
   169	 * Instead: document the ceiling as an explicit, monitorable invariant. At 1,000,000 ids/sec sustained
   170	 * — a rate this schema's actual write paths (gated mutations, one row per HTTP-triggered save) are
   171	 * nowhere near — `2^53 / (1_000_000 * 86_400 * 365)` ≈ 285.6 years. That is not a proof the ceiling can
   172	 * never matter; a future append-only table fed by a genuinely different growth mechanism (e.g. an
   173	 * import job replaying an external system's own id space) must be re-evaluated against this constant
   174	 * explicitly, not assumed safe by association with the tables reviewed here.
   175	 */

   177	  representation: 'bigint(..., { mode: "number" }) — PgBigInt53, routes every read through Number(value)',

   179	  yearsToExhaustAt1MPerSecond: Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER / (1_000_000 * 86_400 * 365),

   182	    "JSON.stringify throws on an un-replaced BigInt, and JS rejects mixed Number/BigInt arithmetic. Both are " +
   183	    "real breakage across the API layer, confirmed independently by two auditors, not a hypothetical risk.",

   441	export type SemanticColumnClass =
   442	  | { readonly kind: "reviewed-id"; readonly growthClass: IdGrowthClass; readonly rationale: string }
   443	  | { readonly kind: "plain-integer" }
   444	  | { readonly kind: "boolean-flag" }

   449	/**
   450	 * The `SQLiteInteger` half of `classifyCoreColumn` — extracted so the top-level switch stays a flat
   451	 * dispatch and this case's own two-step review-then-autoincrement logic reads (and is measured) on
   452	 * its own. Throws if an autoincrement primary key has no entry in `REVIEWED_INTEGER_ID_COLUMNS` — see
   453	 * that registry's own doc for why that is a feature, not a bug: a schema change this manifest has not
   454	 * been updated for must fail loudly here, not silently classify as "must be fine."
   455	 */
   456	function classifyCoreIntegerColumn({ key, col }: { key: string; col: SQLiteColumn }, _optional: Record<string, never> = {}): SemanticColumnClass {
   457	  const review = REVIEWED_INTEGER_ID_COLUMNS[key];
   458	  if (review) return { kind: "reviewed-id", growthClass: review.growthClass, rationale: review.rationale };
   459	  const isAutoIncrementPk = Boolean(col.primary) && Boolean((col as unknown as { autoIncrement?: boolean }).autoIncrement);
   460	  if (isAutoIncrementPk) {

   462	      `autoincrement primary key "${key}" has no entry in REVIEWED_INTEGER_ID_COLUMNS. A new autoincrement ` +
   463	        `column must be explicitly reviewed and assigned a growth class ("unbounded" or "bounded") before this ` +
   464	        `manifest can vouch for it — see that registry's doc for why this fails closed instead of guessing.`
   465	    );

   518	/** Classifies every column of every core table. Throwing anywhere here means the schema has grown a
   519	 * case this manifest has not been reviewed against yet — see `classifyCoreColumn`'s doc. */
   520	export function classifyAllCoreColumns(): ClassifiedColumn[] {
   521	  const out: ClassifiedColumn[] = [];
   522	  for (const { exportName, table } of collectCoreTables()) {
   523	    const cfg = getTableConfig(table);
   524	    const columns = coreColumnsOf(cfg);
   525	    const tsNames = tsPropertyNames(table, columns);

   527	      out.push({
   528	        exportName,
   529	        tsName: tsNames.get(col) ?? col.name,
   530	        sqlTableName: cfg.name,
   531	        sqlColumnName: col.name,
   532	        columnClass: classifyCoreColumn({ sqlTableName: cfg.name, col }),
   533	      });
   534	    }
   535	  }

   564	/**
   565	 * Generates the `setval` statement that must run once, after a bulk copy that preserved the
   566	 * source's original id values and before ANY ordinary insert happens against the target — otherwise
   567	 * Postgres's identity sequence is still at its default starting position and the first ordinary
   568	 * insert collides with (or silently duplicates ahead of) an id the copy already placed.
   569	 *
   570	 * Three cases, all proven live in migration-manifest-postgres.test.ts:
   571	 * - Empty table: next `nextval()` must return `1`.
   572	 * - `max(id) >= 1`: next `nextval()` must return `max(id) + 1` (the ordinary case).
   573	 * - `max(id) < 1` (SQLite's `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` accepts `0` and negative ids, unlike
   574	 *   Postgres's default sequence, whose minimum value is `1`): next `nextval()` must STILL return `1`,
   575	 *   the same as the empty-table case — NOT `max(id) + 1` (which `setval` would reject outright, since
   576	 *   a value below the sequence's minimum is out of bounds) and NOT `2` (a fixed value that would be
   577	 *   wrong for a table that, coincidentally, also has no positive ids yet needs headroom above 1).
   578	 *   Copied rows keep their original non-positive ids untouched either way — only the sequence's
   579	 *   future-allocation position changes, never a stored value.
   580	 *
   581	 * All three cases reduce to one `setval` call: `is_called` is true (allocate strictly above the
   582	 * value passed) only when a real max exists and it is >= 1; otherwise the value passed is `1` and
   583	 * `is_called` is false, so the 3-argument form's `is_called = false` semantics make the NEXT
   584	 * `nextval()` return exactly that `1`, not `2` — the same mechanism the empty-table case already
   585	 * relied on before this function handled non-positive ids too.
   586	 */
   587	export function reseedSequenceSql({ sqlTableName, sqlColumnName }: { sqlTableName: string; sqlColumnName: string }, _optional: Record<string, never> = {}): string {
   588	  assertIdentifierFits({ identifier: sqlTableName, what: `table name` });
   589	  assertIdentifierFits({ identifier: sqlColumnName, what: `column name` });
   590	  const maxExpr = `(SELECT max(${sqlColumnName}) FROM ${sqlTableName})`;
   591	  // NULL (empty table) and any non-positive max both collapse to 0 here, so both take the same
   592	  // "start fresh at 1" path below — the sequence's minimum value is 1, so nothing lower is a legal
   593	  // setval() target regardless of which of those two cases produced it.
   594	  const effectiveMaxExpr = `COALESCE(${maxExpr}, 0)`;
   595	  return (
   596	    `SELECT setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('${sqlTableName}', '${sqlColumnName}'), ` +
   597	    `GREATEST(${effectiveMaxExpr}, 1), ${effectiveMaxExpr} >= 1);`
   598	  );
   599	}

   602	 * The exact clause an INSERT-based bulk copier must add before any INSERT that names an explicit
   603	 * value for a `generatedAlwaysAsIdentity` column (every column `collectIdentityColumns()` returns) —
   604	 * without it, Postgres rejects the INSERT outright: `cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column
   605	 * "id" ... Column "id" is an identity column defined as GENERATED ALWAYS`. Live-verified in
   606	 * migration-manifest-postgres.test.ts.
   607	 *
   608	 * SCOPED TO INSERT-BASED COPIERS ONLY — this is the load-bearing half of this constant, not a
   609	 * footnote. `COPY <table> (id, ...) FROM STDIN` needs NO override syntax at all: `COPY` has no
   610	 * `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE` clause to offer, and none is needed — it writes explicit identity-column
   611	 * values without complaint, live-verified in the same test file. A copier built around `COPY` (the
   612	 * textbook choice for a one-time bulk migration, and the more likely one) that "helpfully" prepends
   613	 * this clause to a COPY statement gets a syntax error, not a safety improvement. Both paths are
   614	 * proven side by side specifically so this asymmetry cannot be rediscovered the hard way by whoever
   615	 * writes the actual copier.
   616	 */
   617	export const IDENTITY_COLUMN_INSERT_OVERRIDE = "OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE" as const;

   620	// 4b. Copy ordering — a topological order derived from the FK graph, so a copier does not have to

   622	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   623	
   624	export interface ForeignKeyEdge {
   625	  /** The table that DECLARES the foreign key (must be copied AFTER `toExportName`). */
   626	  readonly fromExportName: string;
   627	  readonly fromSqlTableName: string;
   628	  /** The table the foreign key POINTS AT (must be copied BEFORE `fromExportName`). */
   629	  readonly toExportName: string;
   630	  readonly toSqlTableName: string;
   631	  /** `true` when a table's own foreign key targets itself (a parent/child hierarchy stored in one
   632	   * table). See `topologicalTableCopyOrder`'s doc for why this is excluded from the returned order
   633	   * rather than resolved by it. */

   637	/**
   638	 * Every foreign key in the core schema, as an edge from the table declaring it to the table it
   639	 * targets — the same `getTableConfig().foreignKeys` / `.reference()` introspection

   641	 * not imported — see this file's module doc on why product code and the `development/scripts/`
   642	 * generator stay decoupled).
   643	 */

   645	  const tables = collectCoreTables();

   647	  const edges: ForeignKeyEdge[] = [];
   648	  for (const { exportName, table } of tables) {
   649	    const cfg = getTableConfig(table);
   650	    for (const fk of cfg.foreignKeys) {
   651	      const ref = (fk as unknown as { reference: () => { foreignTable: object } }).reference();
   652	      const toExportName = exportNameByTable.get(ref.foreignTable);

   654	        throw new Error(

   656	            `cannot be derived without every foreign-key target being a known, exported table.`

   660	        fromExportName: exportName,
   661	        fromSqlTableName: cfg.name,
   662	        toExportName,

   686	interface CopyOrderGraph {

   694	 * non-self-referencing edge, records that `toExportName` has `fromExportName` as a dependent,
   695	 * incrementing `fromExportName`'s in-degree once per distinct table it depends on (a table with

   697	 * needs that target copied before it once, not once per FK column pointing there).

   751	 * duration of that table's copy. That per-table obligation is real and is not discharged by this

   755	  const { dependents, inDegree } = buildCopyOrderGraph(allExportNames, edges);
   756	
   757	  const ready = [...allExportNames].filter((name) => inDegree.get(name) === 0).sort();
   758	  const order: string[] = [];
   759	  const remaining = new Map(inDegree);
   760	  while (ready.length) {
   761	    const next = ready.shift(); // already sorted; shifting keeps output deterministic
   762	    if (next === undefined) throw new Error("table copy order has an empty ready queue");
   763	    order.push(next);
   764	    for (const dependent of dependents.get(next) ?? []) {
   765	      const updated = (remaining.get(dependent) ?? 0) - 1;
   766	      remaining.set(dependent, updated);
   767	      if (updated === 0) insertIntoReadyQueue({ ready, name: dependent });
   768	    }
   769	  }
   770	
   771	  if (order.length !== allExportNames.length) {
   772	    const stuck = allExportNames.filter((name) => !order.includes(name));
   773	    throw new TableCopyOrderCycleError(stuck);
   774	  }
   775	  return order;
   776	}

   778	/** Convenience wrapper: the real core schema's tables, in an order safe for an INSERT/COPY-based
   779	 * bulk copier to walk (referenced tables first). A function, not a module-level constant — see
   780	 * `topologicalTableCopyOrder`'s doc for why a real cycle must fail only the caller that asks for this,
   781	 * never every importer of this module. */
   782	export function computeCoreTableCopyOrder(): string[] {
   783	  const allExportNames = collectCoreTables().map(({ exportName }) => exportName);

# Jini Engine — Locked Architecture & Extraction Plan

Date: 2026-07-16
Status: Architecture LOCKED (Option A + round-2 lock-in fixes). Supersedes `jini-open-design-porting-plan.md`.

Jini = a general-purpose reusable engine extracted from Open Design (OD). OD is the first of many consumers (Open-Marketing, Tovu-Runner, Zana, future products), each in its own repo consuming published `@jini/*` packages. No OD tilt in the engine.

---

## 1. Decision summary

- **Architecture: Option A** — a small neutral kernel + a typed registration contract. Products register providers/tools/packs and supply their own dependency bindings; they never modify the kernel. Affirmed by three independent reviewers (codex gpt-5.6, agy Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude Fable-5).
- **Composition contract: typed DI tokens** (NOT a structural "union of dependency objects"; NOT a reflection/decorator DI container). This was the single biggest correction — a structural intersection decays exactly like OD's `ServerContext` did (40 `any` fields).
- **OD stays a consumer** in its own repo; Jini publishes `@jini/*`; neutrality is *proven* by a packed-tarball `minimal-host` boot in CI, not asserted.
- **OD-sync is a real, enforced patch lane** (hollow re-exports + sync-ownership manifest + a CI patch canary), because "structurally close" is not a sync mechanism — `git format-patch` names exact paths.

## 2. Architecture

### 2.1 Kernel nouns (the true minimum — nothing product-shaped)

`RunLifecycle` · `EventLog`/`EventSink` (replayable: ordering, replay cursor, idempotency key, cancellation) · `AgentExecutor` · `ToolRegistry` + `ToolExecutor` boundary · `ProviderRegistry` (typed tokens) · `Principal`/`Authorizer`. NO projects, artifacts, design-systems, brands, marketplace, conversations in the kernel. Runs key on an opaque `contextRef`, never `projectId`.

### 2.2 Composition contract — typed tokens

```ts
// @jini/core defines tokens (nominal identity + namespacing + version + one|many)
export const RunStore   = token<RunStore>('jini.runStore');
export const EventLog   = token<EventLog>('jini.eventLog');
export const DeployTarget = manyToken<DeployProvider>('jini.deployTarget');

// each feature PACK declares its own deps by token — no global DaemonPorts bag
export const chatPack = definePack({
  deps: [RunStore, EventLog],
  services: (c) => makeChatServices(c.get(RunStore), c.get(EventLog)), // app-services live IN the pack
  http: (app, svc) => app.post('/chat', ...),   // thin; calls svc
  cli:  (reg, svc) => reg.add('chat', ...),      // thin; calls the SAME svc
});

createDaemon({
  packs:    [runsPack(), chatPack(), odDesignPack()],
  bindings: bindings()
    .bind(RunStore, sqlite.runStore(dbPath))
    .bind(EventLog, sqlite.eventLog(dbPath))
    .bind(PrincipalResolver, localPrincipal)
    .bindMany(DeployTarget, netlifyTarget),      // multi-binding, not a central union
  transports: [httpTransport(), cliTransport()],
});
// COMPILE-TIME: Exclude<RequiredTokenIds<packs>, BoundTokenIds<bindings>> must be never
// RUNTIME: startup rejects missing / duplicate-singleton / version-incompatible bindings
//          with a legible message ("missing binding: jini.runStore")
```

Key rules:
- **Kernel exports only kernel-service tokens.** Every other token lives in its owning feature package. Packs may resolve only their declared tokens. No ambient resolver escapes setup. (This is the anti-`ServerContext` guardrail.)
- **Agents and tools are registry entries, not dependency-object fields.**
- **50 tools never enter the composition type.** Only token *ids* are diffed.

### 2.3 Packs own app-services; kernel owns orchestration only

Business logic lives in each feature pack's transport-neutral app-service. `@jini/http` and `@jini/cli` both call those same services (satisfies OD's dual-track contract: UI and CLI hit the same logic). The kernel never accretes feature business logic → it can't become the next `server.ts`.

### 2.4 Host preset (fixes "new consumer must understand the architecture")

```ts
// @jini/node-host — no business nouns; wires sqlite + local eventing + http/sse + cli
createLocalNodeDaemon({ dataDir, packs: [runsPack(), chatPack()], agents: [codexAgentPack()] });
```
A brand-new chat+runs product implements **zero interfaces** to boot.

### 2.5 Tool-execution boundary (a real gate, not a handler getter)

Register `{descriptor, handler, policy}`; invocation is exposed ONLY via `ToolExecutor.execute(principal, run, tool, input, signal)`. Handlers are never publicly retrievable (routes/agents can't bypass authz). Audit covers requested→authorized→confirmed→started→completed→timed-out→cancelled; confirmation is resumable. The confirm/authorize UI is transport-specific, so the transport injects an `ExecutionDelegate` (`onAuthorize`, `onConfirm`) — the headless kernel can't prompt.

### 2.6 Persistence

Ports are **async-only** (Promise-returning) from day one — OD's `db.ts` is sync `better-sqlite3`; a port that copies sync shapes makes Postgres impossible. `@jini/sqlite` is the default adapter (no `@jini/persistence` umbrella). An adapter conformance suite covers transactions/ordering/cursor-durability/cancellation/migrations.

## 3. Locked package set

```
@jini/protocol       pure wire types: run events, errors, cursors, cancellation, idempotency + token TYPE decls
@jini/core           ProviderRegistry, ToolRegistry, DI tokens + resolver, Principal/Authorizer, pure interfaces
@jini/daemon         RunLifecycle, EventLog/EventSink, AgentExecutor, ToolExecutor, createDaemon (stateful)
@jini/agent-runtime  runtimes registry (INSTANCE-based, built-ins generated at build) + defs + stream parsers + discovery
@jini/sqlite         default store adapter behind core/daemon ports
@jini/http           HTTP/SSE transport + route-pack registrar + injects ExecutionDelegate
@jini/cli            CLI transport (HTTP-client mode default; in-proc enters via identical app-service+principal path)
@jini/platform       OS process/file primitives (verbatim lift)
@jini/sidecar        NDJSON-IPC runtime (+ sidecar-proto; identity injected)
@jini/node-host      composition preset (createLocalNodeDaemon); no business nouns
@jini/chat-core      chat pack + app-services + framework-free parsers
@jini/chat-react     refactored ChatPane/ChatComposer → headless hooks + slots (optional)
@jini/renderers-react  artifact/renderer registry + srcDoc sandbox (optional; renamed from artifacts-react for neutrality)
@jini/ui             generic primitives + feature-shaped UI domains + their hooks/providers/ports (optional; renamed from @jini/components 2026-07-16 — one "components" bucket undersold the scope, see packages/ui/README.md)
# deferred until a 2nd host exists: @jini/desktop-host (electron/tauri + RenderService port)
# NOTE (2026-07-17): built ahead of this deferral by explicit human decision, scoped to the
# C7 narrow slice (shell primitives + bridge + RenderService port + Electron/Tauri adapters).
# See packages/desktop-host/source-map.md — a second host consumer is still not confirmed.
```
All React packages are optional. `@jini/core` (pure interfaces/tokens) is split from `@jini/daemon` (stateful lifecycle) so a short-lived CLI can use the tool/registry surface without pulling the daemon runtime.

## 4. OD-sync mechanism (the enforced patch lane)

Requirement: keep absorbing OD's upstream GitHub fixes. `git format-patch` targets exact paths, so:

1. **Hollow re-exports.** The OD adapter (`foundry/integrations/open-design/daemon/…` — corrected 2026-07-17; this doc previously said `products/open-design/daemon/…`, stale from before this repo's `integrations/` rename) **retains OD's exact upstream file tree**. Every file lifted into `@jini/*` is gutted to a 1-line re-export (`export { EventSink } from '@jini/daemon'`). Upstream patches still hit the path.
2. **Sync-ownership manifest.** Maps every upstream daemon path → `product-owned` (patch applies normally, product logic) or `delegated-to-jini` (implementation now lives in a package).
3. **Patch canary in CI (permanent).** Applies representative real upstream patches with a tested directory transform (`apps/daemon/… → foundry/integrations/open-design/daemon/…`). A patch touching a `delegated-to-jini` path **fails CI** until the equivalent `@jini/*` package patch + conformance test land — this prevents a fix applying to a *dead compatibility copy* while the running impl stays vulnerable.
4. **Strangler-fig OD adapter.** Mount OD's Express app whole behind `createDaemon` first; migrate a route group to a pack only after a churn audit (git-log frequency) shows upstream rarely touches it. Patchability is the default; pack-migration is the earned exception.

## How a feature runs
1. A filler script (`scripts/make-sheet.py`, step W0.3) fills the mechanical fields of the sheet: blobs, census hits (`scripts/census.py`), `non_reexport_statements`, the baseline search (`rg -F <path>` over `*.json`/`*.mjs`/`*.cjs`/`*.yml`), the declaration list, Jini guards, the lines next to the exports, and whether a name already exists. It WRITES the sheet to `sheets/<kind>-<slug>.md` before any edit, so a discovery made while executing shows up as a change to a saved sheet (W0: the observability sheet was written after the edit).
2. The tier in `slice_tiers` decides who fills the judgment fields: `Sonnet` fills them (about 12k + 12 tokens per line); `Sonnet+review` has Sonnet fill them and Opus check the split and ports (about 8k + 4 tokens per line of Opus); `Opus` fills them (about 15k + 20 tokens per line).
3. Sonnet 5.5 high executes the assembled recipe from the SAVED sheet (`cat T-<KIND>.md sheets/<kind>-<slug>.md COMMON.md`), one slice per job: a Jini commit then a Tovu commit. An executor never edits before the sheet file exists. A STOP gives a clean SKIP. Within a feature, slices run in the order REPOINT, DELETE, HARDEN, MOVE, DEDUPE, UI, SPLIT, SERVER.
4. Verification happens in one batched cloud run per wave (single-runner rule). It covers the RED/GREEN checks for failing-test-first rows, the Jini gates (subpath isolation, hardwiring, complexity, size) and Tovu typecheck after linking the Tovu clone to `jini-terra-base` (D1 default: linked). UI slices also need a Chrome look.

item.text: Software Architect(Direct): I found two useful distinctions. Jini already owns the error envelope, status mapping, and serializer; Tovu’s helper adds its request-correlation policy. The migration manifest combines Tovu schema decisions with a reusable ordering algorithm, while Jini already owns database-copy and sequence-reseeding behavior. That points toward keeping host policy and extracting only the missing shared behavior.

# GOV-ADR-003: DDL Generation Never Interpolates Operator-Supplied Input

- **Status:** ACCEPTED
- **Enforcement:** MANDATORY
- **Date:** 2026-07-15
- **Author:** Software Architect (Claude Sonnet 5, Agent Direct Mode)
- **Scope Globs:** `src/features/content-types/**; src/infra/**`

## Rule

Any code path that generates SQL DDL from operator-supplied metadata MUST handle it by exactly one of two mechanisms, chosen by the value's shape — no third mechanism is permitted:

1. **Closed-vocabulary metadata** (a field `kind`, a collation, a namespace selector — any value drawn from a small, fixed, developer-controlled enum) MUST route through a fixed, closed, core-owned lookup table that maps it to a pre-approved SQL literal — never interpolated, even after validation.
2. **Free-text identifiers** (a field name, a content-type key, or any other operator-chosen, effectively unbounded string) MUST pass a strict identifier grammar (e.g. `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,63}$`) before appearing in a DDL **identifier position** — an index name segment, or a JSON-path key segment inside the one sanctioned path-literal template (e.g. the `<name>` segment of `'$.<name>'` inside a `json_extract(...)` call). A grammar-validated identifier MUST NEVER appear anywhere else: not in a type position, not in an arbitrary string literal, not concatenated into any other clause. The JSON-path-literal placement is a controlled position, not free-form SQL content — the grammar's excluded characters (quote, backslash, dot, bracket, whitespace, statement separators) make it impossible for a grammar-passed identifier to escape that one templated position. A grammar-validated identifier is not a lookup-table entry — it is still operator-authored text, so it may only ever occupy one of these named positions, never anywhere the surrounding DDL would treat it as executable SQL content beyond that template.

A fixed lookup table cannot express mechanism 2 by construction (field names are an unbounded set) — do not attempt to force free-text identifiers through the lookup-table mechanism; use the grammar-gate mechanism for them instead.

Identity encoding for anything built by joining two or more grammar-gated identifiers (e.g. an index name derived from a content-type key plus a field name) MUST use a delimiter character outside the grammar's own alphabet (e.g. `/`, never `_`) — otherwise two distinct `(key, name)` pairs can encode to the same joined string, which is a namespace-injectivity defect independent of DDL-injection (same defect class as `ADS-memory/reports/architecture/ADR-026-*.md`'s atomic-write namespace-injectivity finding).

## Why

Collections (SPEC-020) lets an operator define arbitrary content-type fields with a `kind` that ultimately drives an index's `CAST(... AS {sqlType})` DDL, AND a field `name` that becomes part of the index's own identity/extraction path. A validate-then-interpolate approach for the `kind` value (allow-list check, then build the DDL string from the validated value) makes the safety property depend on the validator being correct forever — a validator bug, typo, or future relaxation could silently reopen a SQL-injection-shaped vulnerability. A fixed lookup table makes that half of the property structural: there is no code path where `kind` text reaches a DDL string at all. This was decided during SPEC-020's Software Architect pass (ADR-PIPE-020), explicitly rejecting the validate-then-interpolate alternative for `kind` for this exact reason.

**Correction (2026-07-15, `/audit-work` round 1 — three independent auditors, Fable/Codex/Gemini, all independently converged on this):** the original Rule text applied the closed-lookup-table requirement to field *names* as well as `kind`, which is unsatisfiable — a fixed table cannot enumerate an unbounded set of operator-chosen names. SPEC-020's own actual design was already correct (REQ-03's grammar check runs before any DDL is constructed, per AC-05), but this governance ADR's Rule as originally worded did not reflect that second, distinct mechanism, and SPEC-020's own CIC U-001 designated only the `kind`→CAST lookup, leaving field-name DDL-safety undesignated anywhere. Both are fixed as of this revision — see the Rule's two-track mechanism above and SPEC-020's CIC U-001-B2 (`ADS-memory/reports/pipeline/020-collections/critical-internal-constraints.md`).

**Correction (2026-07-15, `/audit-work` round 2 — Fable and Codex independently converged on this):** the round-1 fix's own wording was internally contradictory — it named a JSON-path key as a permitted identifier position while separately banning any appearance "inside a string literal," but SPEC-020 REQ-04/REQ-06's actual required construction (`CAST(json_extract(fieldsJson, '$.<name>') AS <sqlType>)`) necessarily places the field name inside a single-quoted string literal. Both auditors independently confirmed the grammar gate (excluding quote/backslash/dot/bracket/whitespace/separator characters) makes this placement safe regardless — the defect was in the Rule's taxonomy, not the underlying mechanism. Fixed by naming the JSON-path-literal placement as the one sanctioned string-literal position above. Also added in this round: a delimiter-injectivity requirement for joined identity encodings (Fable's independent finding, not part of round 1's ledger) — see the Rule's final paragraph.

## Enforcement

- [ ] Linter rule: N/A — no static signature reliably distinguishes safe lookup-table/grammar-gate use from a validated-but-interpolated string.
- [ ] CI check: none yet.
- [x] Code review checklist item — Code Review Agent treats (a) any closed-vocabulary DDL-generation code path not routing through the fixed lookup table, (b) any free-text identifier appearing anywhere other than an index-name segment or the sanctioned JSON-path-literal key position, and only after passing the strict grammar gate, or (c) any joined identity encoding using a delimiter inside the grammar's own alphabet, as a Required (blocking) finding.
- [x] adr-governance skill path-match lookup — any change under the scope globs resolves this ADR.
- [ ] Manual review only.

## Comply-or-Explain (DEFAULT rules only)

N/A — MANDATORY, no comply-or-explain path.

## Consequences

**Positive:** DDL-injection is structurally impossible for any covered code path, not merely validated against.

**Negative:** Adding a new field kind or DDL-relevant type requires a core code change to the lookup table, not just an operator-facing extension.

## Re-evaluation Triggers

- A future domain needs a DDL-generation pattern the fixed-lookup-table approach cannot express.
- 3+ exceptions recorded against this rule within 90 days.

## Related

- Origin: `ADS-memory/reports/pipeline/020-collections/adr.md` (ADR-PIPE-020)
- Supersedes: none
- See also: GOV-ADR-001, GOV-ADR-002

item.text: Software Architect(Direct): My recommendations are taking shape: keep the Tovu error-policy helper; establish one shared event contract and move stateful adapters to infra; split reusable migration ordering from the site manifest; and move reusable MCP service behavior while retaining Tovu’s response and security policy. I’m checking the existing contract assertions for any behavior those moves must preserve.

Software Architect(Direct): Recommend **KEEP, CONSOLIDATE/SPLIT, SPLIT, SPLIT**, respectively. No files were edited; no tests or builds were run. C3b was inspected at `f5d9f84` through its existing local ref. Contract changes below are proposals.

**1. `server/error-mapping`**

**RECOMMENDATION:** Keep `respondToApiError` as Tovu’s shared HTTP policy adapter; extract nothing further now.

**WHY**

- Jini already owns the reusable behavior: error construction, default status mapping, and envelope serialization. Tovu’s helper calls those owners. See [respond.ts:3](/Users/la/Programming/tovu-codex-trial-terra/apps/website/src/server/error-mapping/respond.ts:3), [statusForError:59](/Users/la/Programming/jini-terra-base/packages/core/src/contracts/server/api-error.ts:59), and [sendApiError:19](/Users/la/Programming/jini-terra-base/packages/http-kit/src/response.ts:19).
- Its remaining responsibility is meaningful host policy: read Tovu’s established correlation ID and omit it when absent. Request tracking creates that context separately. See [respond.ts:13](/Users/la/Programming/tovu-codex-trial-terra/apps/website/src/server/error-mapping/respond.ts:13) and [observability-middleware.ts:81](/Users/la/Programming/tovu-codex-trial-terra/apps/website/src/server/inbound/shared/observability-middleware.ts:81).
- Folding it into analytics would assign a shared transport policy to a feature route. The recorded migration inventory spans many route families, although each still needs individual contract review. See [INFO.md:73](/Users/la/Programming/tovu-codex-trial-terra/apps/website/src/server/error-mapping/INFO.md:73).
- Express is **not itself a reason extraction is impossible**: Jini already accepts a structural `ApiErrorResponseWriter`. The reason to retain this helper is its host convention and the absence of additional unowned generic behavior. See [response.ts:8](/Users/la/Programming/jini-terra-base/packages/http-kit/src/response.ts:8).

**CONCRETE SHAPE:** Keep Tovu’s existing `respondToApiError({ res, code, message }, { details })`. Routes supply reviewed copy and safe details; request middleware supplies correlation context. Import `createApiError` from `@jini-ai/protocol`, `statusForError` directly from `@jini-ai/core/contracts/server`, and `sendApiError` from `@jini-ai/http-kit`. Add no Jini factory, compatibility export, or replacement wrapper.

**RISKS / WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER:** A second host needing configurable correlation extraction could justify extending the existing HTTP response owner. Do not automatically apply this JSON policy to OAuth, MCP, or streaming responses; the current policy explicitly preserves their protocol formats. See [INFO.md:85](/Users/la/Programming/tovu-codex-trial-terra/apps/website/src/server/error-mapping/INFO.md:85).

**CONFIDENCE:** High.

**2. `contracts/core/events`**

**RECOMMENDATION:** Make `@jini-ai/core/contracts/events` the single shared contract owner, reconcile its contract with infra’s stronger lease semantics, and move stateful implementations to infra.

**WHY**

- C3b fixes contract placement but preserves the old positional enqueue and implicit lease. Infra’s contract explicitly passes `claimLeaseMs`, supports generic envelopes, and carries optional claim tokens. These are behavioral differences, not naming differences. See [core events ports:111](/Users/la/Programming/jini-terra-base/packages/core/src/contracts/events/ports.ts:111) and [infra ports.ts:3](/Users/la/Programming/jini-terra-base/packages/infra/src/events/outbox/ports.ts:3).
- Tovu currently reconciles two Jini contracts itself, including discarding the worker’s per-call lease argument. Every future host should not inherit this translation obligation. See [jini-outbox-adapter.ts:18](/Users/la/Programming/tovu-codex-trial-terra/apps/website/src/contracts/core/events/jini-outbox-adapter.ts:18).
- Lease duration participates in correctness: infra validates that it exceeds the full batch timeout budget. Adopting the old core shape verbatim would leave that agreement implicit. See [policy.ts:18](/Users/la/Programming/jini-terra-base/packages/infra/src/events/outbox/policy.ts:18).
- The in-memory bus and outbox own mutable subscriptions and delivery state. They belong with reusable infrastructure implementations, outside pure core and outside CMS-specific ownership. See [memory-bus.ts:22](/Users/la/Programming/tovu-codex-trial-terra/apps/website/src/contracts/core/events/memory-bus.ts:22).
- Tovu genuinely owns event-to-policy composition and process selection. Its retry table combines forms and webhook behavior; its serving root starts delivery after app construction. See [outbox-retry-policies.ts:17](/Users/la/Programming/tovu-codex-trial-terra/apps/website/src/contracts/core/events/outbox-retry-policies.ts:17) and [serving-app.ts:75](/Users/la/Programming/tovu-codex-trial-terra/apps/website/src/server/runtime/composition/serving-app.ts:75).

**CONCRETE SHAPE:**

- **`@jini-ai/core/contracts/events`:** Own `DomainEvent`, `EventPublisher`, `EventBusPort`, generic `OutboxRecord<Event>`, `OutboxClaim`, `OutboxPort<Event>`, and shared `OutboxRetryPolicy` / `OutboxRetryPolicyResolver`. Normalize methods to `(requiredArgs, optionalArgs = {})`; enqueue and publish receive `{ event }`. Claims explicitly receive `{ batchSize, nowIso, claimLeaseMs }`; settlement preserves optional fencing receipts.
- Preserve required `DomainEvent.workspaceId`. Keep the worker generic over a smaller envelope so non-CMS hosts need not manufacture CMS fields. The current tenant requirement is explicit. See [core events ports:31](/Users/la/Programming/jini-terra-base/packages/core/src/contracts/events/ports.ts:31).
- **`@jini-ai/infra/events/outbox`:** Own `processOutbox`, `startOutboxDrainer`, `toEnqueueOnlyOutbox`, policies/defaults, scheduling, and `InMemoryOutbox`. Put `InMemoryEventBus` in an infra events leaf. These implementations consume core contracts directly.
- **Host wiring:** Supply durable storage, subscribed bus, clock, scheduler, randomness, safe logging/tracing, and the event-specific retry resolver. Update Tovu’s SQL adapter to honor the passed lease while preserving its existing row format and default behavior. Its current lease is constructor-bound. See [outbox-repo.ts:78](/Users/la/Programming/tovu-codex-trial-terra/apps/website/src/platform/db/repos/outbox-repo.ts:78).
- **Tovu retains:** Schema/repository binding, subscriber registration, retry-policy selection, observability decoration, delivery-process ownership, and shutdown orchestration. Delete translation adapters and forwarding exports after consumers import their actual owners.

**RISKS / WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER:** This requires an explicit amendment to C3’s “verbatim” contract decision before implementation. Preserve envelope contents, idempotent enqueue, atomic claims, retry decisions, and late-outcome behavior. Optional claim tokens do not provide the stronger guarantees of the separate `FencedOutboxPort` protocol; retain that distinction. Existing unfenced late-write risk is documented in [worker.ts:150](/Users/la/Programming/jini-terra-base/packages/infra/src/events/outbox/worker.ts:150). Land contract/implementation reconciliation before the consumer repoint.

**CONFIDENCE:** High on ownership; medium on the exact compatibility migration.

**3. `platform/db/migration`**

**RECOMMENDATION:** Keep the schema manifest in Tovu, but extract reusable table-copy ordering into Jini’s existing database-transfer owner.

**WHY**

- The manifest introspects Tovu’s concrete Drizzle schema and records product judgments about particular columns. Those facts cannot become a neutral platform schema. See [manifest.ts:66](/Users/la/Programming/tovu-codex-trial-terra/apps/website/src/platform/db/migration/manifest.ts:66) and [REVIEWED_JSON_COLUMNS:390](/Users/la/Programming/tovu-codex-trial-terra/apps/website/src/platform/db/migration/manifest.ts:390).
- `topologicalTableCopyOrder` is already separated from schema discovery and runs over supplied names and edges. Its deterministic ordering and cycle handling are reusable behavior. See [manifest.ts:736](/Users/la/Programming/tovu-codex-trial-terra/apps/website/src/platform/db/migration/manifest.ts:736).
- Jini already owns transfer metadata, copying, and sequence-reseeding behavior. Extend that owner rather than creating another migration subsystem. See [transfer/index.ts:1](/Users/la/Programming/jini-terra-base/packages/db/src/transfer/index.ts:1) and [internal-ddl.ts:65](/Users/la/Programming/jini-terra-base/packages/db/src/transfer/internal-ddl.ts:65).
- The host already injects its schema, order, and derived-object exclusions into transfer composition. That is the correct boundary to preserve.
